prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened a new regime of accuracy in frequency measurement

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B005 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye. The claim rests on one conceptual step and its realisation: choose the lattice wavelength so that the light shift of the clock transition cancels, then interrogate a very large number of atoms free of Doppler and recoil effects. That step changes the statistical and systematic budget of an optical clock, and it carried fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. It has been reproduced and surpassed with strontium, ytterbium and other species in several countries, and clock comparisons now constrain relativistic geodesy and drifts of constants. The chair asks for an explicit criterion between B005 and B014. Mine is whether a stated, checkable achievement is mature enough and attributable to the proposed names without a cut that the record would contradict. On that test B005 is the more secure of the two. On the chair's question about Ye, I would word the credit as the realisation of the lattice clock at record accuracy and its extension into the many-body regime, with Katori credited for the magic-wavelength concept and first lattice spectroscopy; the citation I propose says invention and realisation without ranking the two contributions. I would keep the wording tied to the lattice and to accuracy, and not to precision timekeeping in general or to ultrastable lasers.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and I do not think the exchange has removed it: the area neighbours the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, and a committee that wants conceptual surprise more than improved precision could reasonably call a third prize here incremental. The two-name credit also leaves out other lattice-clock groups, in particular the Paris and PTB efforts, and the ultrastable-laser developers, and fine priority between the Tokyo and Boulder work, and who first published the magic-wavelength proposal, are points that colleagues and I have only from memory and should be checked against the primary papers before the names are fixed. The payoff through a redefinition of the second remains prospective. Finally B014 has a broader effect across condensed-matter physics, and I cannot claim that a measurement-science prize is the better use of the slot on scientific grounds alone.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B014 and argues that the theory-to-experiment line from the 2011 continuum model to the 2018 discovery is unusually clean, that confirmation was fast, and that nothing is gained by waiting.
responses.response: I accept that the prediction-then-discovery structure is unusually clean and that the reproduction was fast, and B014 stays my first alternative. Two things keep me from moving. First, the credit: Eriksson himself says that Cao's lead-author role and the earlier twisted-bilayer band theory of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto cannot be settled from the supplied names and rest on recollection, so a three-name list may need to change after checking. Second, the open pairing mechanism does not undermine the discovery of correlated states, as he argues, but it does mean the field's own account of what was found is still moving. I do not claim that B014 is premature, only that its case is currently less settled than B005 on the specific questions of credit and interpretation. If a check of the primary record settled the credit, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Mehlig frames the choice as a new-phenomenon prize (B014) against a measurement-science prize (B005) and asks whether a clock is a discovery about nature or an instrument achievement.
responses.response: I think the framing is useful but I do not accept that it favours B014 automatically. The criterion is the discovery or invention that has conferred the greatest benefit, and the lattice clock is an invention in the plain sense: the magic wavelength is a new idea that did not exist before, and it opened measurements that had not been possible, including height differences from gravitational redshift and sensitive bounds on varying constants. A new instrument that creates a new regime of measurement is not a lesser category than a new phase of matter. I do agree with him that the instrument claim must be shown to be more than a better number, which is why my citation names the lattice trapping and not the accuracy alone. I also note that he moved to B014 after accepting all three names, and that he acknowledges the maturity worry, which on the second point we read differently.

responses.point: Danielsson says he is close to indifferent between B005 and B014, worries that B005 is incremental next to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and asks whether Ye's role is co-invention or record-accuracy realisation.
responses.response: On redundancy, I would say that the 2005 prize rewarded the comb that counts optical cycles and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions, whereas the lattice clock rests on trapping neutral atoms in large numbers at a magic wavelength, which is a different physical route to a different limiting uncertainty. Those two prizes made it readable and usable, so I regard them as context and not as prior recognition of the same thing. I do not claim to have a complete answer, since ion clocks also reach very low uncertainty. On Ye, I would treat the contribution as realisation at record accuracy together with the exploration of many-body effects in the lattice, and I do not think the committee needs to call it co-invention to justify a pair. Danielsson asks for a criterion, and I would say it should be that the citation can be written so that each credited name matches a distinct, checkable step.

responses.point: Kroll supports B005 but concedes that B014 draws broader support, that fine priority among the early magic-wavelength proposals and first lattice spectroscopy should be checked, and that he disclosed a stay in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree with his candour about the priority record and I think it is the most important open item for B005: who first proposed magic-wavelength trapping, who first showed lattice spectroscopy, and what the parallel strontium and ytterbium efforts contributed should be checked against primary papers before the names are fixed. Where I differ from him slightly is on breadth of support. He treats the Borda lead of B014 as a serious competitor; I read support counts as evidence about the committee's opinions and not about the science, and the chair rightly asks us not to use them as a substitute. I also note that his disclosure and my own adjacency to the field are the same kind of proximity, so we should both be tested by colleagues on whether we are overweighting precision arguments.

uncertainties: Priority among early magic-wavelength proposals and first lattice spectroscopy, and the role of the Paris, PTB and other strontium and ytterbium groups, rest on recollection and should be checked against the primary papers.
Whether a third prize near precision spectroscopy after 2005 and 2012 is acceptable, or whether B014 should be chosen for its broader effect on the field.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing, which I think it should not.
Whether I overweight a precision-atomic-physics argument because of my own field.
Whether the three-name credit for B014 would survive a check of the earlier twisted-bilayer theory and Cao's role, in which case my ranking of the two ballots could change.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. My profile documents no personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye. My documented connections are to Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Ingvar Lindgren's Gothenburg group, and Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, and none of them is a credited name for B005. I am a theoretical atomic physicist in a field adjacent to B005 and I record that proximity as a possible bias toward precision-atomic arguments. No specific conflict or recusal issue is apparent.
